title: Using a Multiple-Choice Assessment to Examine Misconceptions in Maths
author: Patrick Barmby
summary: This No More Marking post opens a series reporting on a year-long Axiom Maths/No More Marking research project tracking Year 7 mathematics progress, starting with the initial multiple-choice assessment results. Using a 15-item diagnostic drawn from Craig Barton's own bank of diagnostic questions, researchers tested 1,789 students across 17 partnership schools and then analysed not just how many students got each item right, but which specific wrong answer (distractor) they chose. The post walks through several worked examples: a place-value item where lower-scoring students consistently misread "fifty-three hundredths" as "fifty-three hundred," and a fraction-subtraction item where the dominant wrong answer showed students subtracting numerators and denominators directly rather than converting to a common denominator first. The authors use these patterns to argue that distractor analysis surfaces specific, addressable misconceptions that a simple percentage-correct score would hide entirely, since two students with the same score might be making completely different errors. The post closes by flagging a follow-up piece on the same students' comparative-judgement assessment results, positioning this multiple-choice analysis as the first half of a two-part diagnostic picture of the same Year 7 cohort.
points: The Axiom Maths/No More Marking project ran a 15-item multiple-choice diagnostic (drawn from Craig Barton's own question bank) with nearly 1,800 Year 7 students across 17 schools, analysing not just correctness but which wrong answer students picked.

Distractor analysis on a place-value item found low-scoring students systematically read "fifty-three hundredths" as "fifty-three hundred," a specific and correctable misconception invisible in a simple right/wrong mark.

On a fraction-subtraction item, the dominant wrong answer revealed students subtracting numerators and denominators directly without finding a common denominator first - a textbook procedural misconception rather than random error.

The team explicitly frames wrong-answer patterns as more diagnostically useful than raw scores, since the same score can hide very different underlying misconceptions depending on which distractor a student chose.
quotes: In this post, we examine the initial results from the multiple-choice assessment, in particular looking at the analysis of distractor items for particular questions, and what insight this analysis can provide about student misconceptions.
In total 1789 students from 17 schools completed the multiple-choice assessment.

The lowest scoring students were most likely to choose response A, 5300, perhaps interpreting fifty-three hundredths as fifty-three hundred. Students in the middle range of scores were most likely to choose response D, 0.053.

The lower to middle scoring students were most likely to choose response, three quarters. We can see the misconception that they simply subtracted the numerators and the denominators without converting the fractions to a common denominator.

This item is shown as an example because we can see that there were no likely distractors in this case — everyone was likely to choose option A, therefore very few students showed any misconception for this item.
